titre: The Rule Against the Final Preposition
accroche: “Never end an English sentence with a preposition” isn't a rule of grammar: it's the vexed taste of one poet, in 1672.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1672, the poet and playwright John Dryden published an essay defending his own play, *Defence of the Epilogue*, appended to *The Conquest of Granada*. In it he settles scores with his rival Ben Jonson, dead since 1637, and picks out in Jonson's play *Catiline* (1611) a sentence describing souls so frightened that there were not enough wild beasts left to devour *the bodies that those souls were frighted from* (the bodies those souls had fled). Dryden's verdict fits on a line: “The Preposition in the end of the sentence; a common fault with him.” He nowhere explains why it would be one.

## A Remark of Taste, Turned Rule

Dryden isn't quite isolated: a more obscure grammarian, Joshua Poole, had voiced a comparable reservation a few decades earlier, in a little-read manual. But it's Dryden's remark, signed by the most prominent literary critic of his day, that spreads. More revealing still: researchers who have compared successive editions of his own plays show that he afterward went back to his earlier texts to move the prepositions; he retroactively corrects his own pen to conform to a rule he has just invented by criticizing someone else.

## A Loan from Latin, Not a Law of English

The reason underlying this kind of judgment, in Dryden as in the grammarians who would take up the rule in the 18th century, lies in the prestige of Latin. In Latin, a preposition governs a noun that must follow it within the same phrase: the structure of the language makes a final preposition simply impossible. Generations of grammarians, convinced that Latin embodied the very logic of language, wanted to impose this constraint on English, a language where prepositions work quite differently, and where they have been detached from their complements since Anglo-Saxon, long before Dryden. The linguist Geoffrey Pullum is categorical on this point: such sentences are not grammatical errors, and never were.

## What This Shifts

The episode shows how a personal preference, propped up by the prestige of a foreign language, can be transmitted as a timeless law of correctness, to the point that generations of schoolchildren rewrote perfectly natural sentences to avoid a “fault” that a 17th-century poet pointed out without ever justifying it, never suspecting that we would still have him to thank for it three and a half centuries later.

carte.punch: Ending a sentence with a preposition, a mistake? Dryden writes it in 1672, without saying why.
carte.idee: In 1672, John Dryden faults Ben Jonson for ending a sentence with a preposition, without saying why, then revises his own texts to conform. Joshua Poole had voiced a comparable reservation; the model is Latin, where a final preposition is impossible.

quiz.question: Where does the rule forbidding ending an English sentence with a preposition come from?
choix: From a Latin grammar rule directly inherited by English during the Norman Conquest
From a 19th-century linguistic study that supposedly demonstrated that this construction harms clarity
From a remark of taste by the poet John Dryden in 1672, drawing on an ideal of logic modeled on Latin, with no grammatical justification
From a rule issued by an English Academy of the language in the 18th century, on the model of the French Academy
quiz.explication: In 1672, Dryden criticizes a sentence of Ben Jonson's without justifying his judgment; the preference rests on the prestige of Latin, where a final preposition is structurally impossible, but not on any English grammatical rule, this construction having existed since Old English. There is no English Academy of the language comparable to the French Academy, no 19th-century study demonstrating a lack of clarity, and no direct inheritance from Norman.
